High pressure will remain anchored offshore through Wednesday 
while a frontal system stalled over the Great Lakes and interior 
Northeast starts a slow southeastward drift. This will result in 
near record temperatures. Even though dew points will also be 
rising, the large spread with the temperatures will result in 
afternoon RH in the 30s and 40s. Southwesterly winds will also 
remain gusty, especially today.
The front will drop southward Wednesday, then stall nearby or 
overhead Thursday, increasing the potential for showers and
thunderstorms. There will also be a large contrast in temperatures
from northeast to southwest across the area.
The front will lift northward as a warm front Friday ahead of a 
strong cold front approaching from the west. The next opportunity
for more numerous showers and perhaps some thunderstorms will 
occur with this front on Sunday.

can not be ruled out with the front passing, but conditions appear less 
supportive of this activity. Winds turn northerly once the front passes,
generally ranging between 10-15 mph initially, but then increasing to
15-20 mph by around 10 PM. Gusty winds are likely through the remainder of 
the night once this occurs and could eventually tip more northeast in direction
late. Dry high pressure is forecast to build over the region on Tuesday. Northeast
winds between 10 to 15 mph should advect dewpoints in the 30s across the burn 
site on Tuesday. As a result, relative humidity values are forecast to 
drop into the mid-upper 30s Tuesday afternoon.

dropping to between 30-35 percent.  Skies will be mostly sunny,
with possibly some thin cirrus passing across the region through
the afternoon hours.  Finally, although fog is not expected

passage from earlier in the morning. RH values could drop into 
the upper teens to 20s across much of the area. Winds will be

front, which looks to bring wetting rains Sunday evening/night.

the impacts of some gusty southeasterly flow (20-30 mph gusts). 
Showers and thunderstorms look likely on Monday before strong west-
northwesterly winds overspread the area Monday evening into
Tuesday. High pressure returns by the middle of next week.

corridor, where 15-25 mph wind gusts can be expected.

.DISCUSSION...
Today and Saturday look somewhat concerning in regards to fire 
weather, although fuel moisture will be a limiting factor.
Except for some isolated areas in the Shenandoah Valley and Potomac 
Highlands, most of the area will have received a quarter inch of 
precipitation over the past couple of days.
With that said, a dry frontal system will be approaching the region 
today before moving through tonight. Ahead of that, very 
strong southerly winds pick up. The air mass will be extremely dry, 
and could be locally enhanced in downslope flow west of the Blue 
Ridge. Current forecast has low to mid 30s RHs in the typical drier 
valleys with low 40s at higher elevations. 
Saturday may actually be the driest day, behind the frontal passage 
from tonight. RH values could drop into the teens to 20s across 
much of the area. Winds will be on the decline, but will remain 
somewhat elevated, especially along/north of the interstate 66 
corridor, where 15-25 mph wind gusts can be expected.
Gusty winds but increasing RHs are forecast Sunday ahead of another 
front, which looks to bring wetting rains Sunday evening/night. 
There is less of a threat Sunday, but any ongoing fires could feel 
the impacts of some gusty southeasterly flow (20-25 mph gusts).
